title: Writing a will
hookLine: a Muslim shouldn't spend two nights without a written will (Bukhari)

cards: That's the window in this hadith, and it's short on purpose. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar reports it, in Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase, that it isn't right for a Muslim who has something to leave in a will to spend two nights without that will written down and kept with them.
Not someday, once things settle down. Two nights. And in Sahih Muslim, Ibn 'Umar adds what he did about it: from the time he heard those words, not a single night passed without his will beside him.

teach.b: The word is wasiyyah: a will, a bequest, and also a charge, the last instructions you leave in someone's care.
In surah al-Baqarah, those near death who leave wealth are told to make a bequest for parents and near relatives, fairly, as a duty on those who are mindful of God.
The Qur'an also names fixed shares for heirs, in surah al-Nisa, which is tomorrow's story. The wasiyyah is the part a person shapes for themselves, and a hadith puts a limit on it.
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas tells it, also in al-Bukhari. He was ill, and the Prophet came to visit. Sa'd said he had wealth, and only a daughter to inherit, and asked: may I give away all of it in my will?

teach.h: A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.
teach.b: And the Prophet said, in paraphrase: a third, and a third is a lot. It's better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them poor, holding out their hands to people.
So a will carries two loves at once: for the causes and people outside the family, and for the family, who shouldn't be left in need. Why the hurry? The hadith doesn't say.
One way to hear it: nobody knows which night is the last. A will written today isn't gloomy. It's kind.
The people you love won't spend their grief guessing, or arguing, about what you wanted.

how: Muslims are encouraged to keep a written will, a wasiyyah, citing the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in al-Bukhari; bequests outside the fixed shares of inheritance are limited to a third of the estate, following the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

o: a will: the bequest and last charge you leave in others' care
a prayer said at the bedside of someone who is dying
the fixed shares the Qur'an sets for each heir in a family

p: not a night without his will
asked to give all of it away
and a third is a lot

s: the hadith says a will can wait until you're old
it speaks of not spending two nights without a written will.
the Prophet let Sa'd give away all of his wealth in his will
he said no to all and to half, and said: a third, and a third is a lot.
the reason given was that heirs shouldn't be left in need
better to leave your heirs well off than poor, holding out their hands.

games.q: you're Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, ill, with wealth and one daughter to inherit. what do you ask the Prophet?
o: can I leave nothing to anyone?
can I give all of it away in my will?
games.why: he asked to give all, then half; the Prophet allowed a third, saying a third is a lot and heirs shouldn't be left in need.

practice: Ask yourself: if this were my last night, what would the people I love need to know? Where things are kept, who should be looked after, any debt to repay or promise to keep, any cause you'd want to share in what you leave.
Where you live, the law may have its own requirements, so this is only the first page of a will, in your head.

wordCard.voice: Wasiyyah. A will and a final charge, written so the people you leave behind have peace. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a will, a bequest, a charge left in someone's care.

carryVoice: Your line: write it. Their peace, after you, is what it protects. See you tomorrow.
